title: Understand Dough Instead of Following Recipes
lede: Dough is the most rewarding system in the kitchen for a precision-minded cook: four ingredients — flour, water, salt, leavening — plus one hidden variable, time, expressed in baker's percentages, produce everything from Neapolitan pizza to a 30-hour sourdough.

blocks.html: A recipe is a single sampled point on a continuous surface. It tells you "500 g flour, 325 g water, bake at 220 °C" but never tells you what happens if your kitchen is 10 °C colder, if your flour is stronger, or if you want twelve pizzas instead of four. You end up cargo-culting numbers you don't understand, and when the dough misbehaves you have no model to debug it with.

The dial-in you already know from espresso maps directly onto dough. In coffee you have dose, yield, grind, temperature and time, and you learn that ratios travel between machines while absolute grams do not. Dough is the same: baker's percentages are the ratio recipe, hydration is your extraction lever, fermentation time-and-temperature is your roast development, and salt is the fixed constant you never skip. Learn the four variables and their trade-offs and you stop reading recipes as commandments and start reading them as data points you can interpolate between.

The payoff is concrete and fast. The single change that turns "fine home pizza" into "why does this taste like the good pizzeria" is not a secret ingredient — it is a 48-hour cold ferment, a free lever most recipes bury. By the end of this module you should be able to write your own dough spec for any target crumb, scale it to any batch size, and diagnose a failure from the dough's behaviour rather than guessing.

items.label: L1 — I can make edible bread and pizza that rises
L2 — I reproduce the same crumb on demand, batch to batch
L3 — I tune hydration, ferment and shape for a target result
L4 — I write specs from scratch and run a sourdough culture

sections.title: Mental model — dough as a gas-retention system

blocks.html: Strip dough to its function and it is a machine for generating gas and trapping it. Yeast (or the wild culture in a starter) ferments sugars into CO2; a protein network built from wheat's gluten catches that gas in thousands of separate cells; the oven then flash-expands the gas and locks the walls in place. Every technique you will ever learn is serving one of two jobs: build the net (gluten development) or fill it with gas at the right rate (fermentation). Salt, hydration, shaping and the bake are the tuning knobs on those two jobs.

Gluten itself is two proteins that behave like opposite springs. Glutenin gives elasticity and strength — it wants to snap back. Gliadin gives extensibility and flow — it wants to stretch and stay. Dry, they do nothing. Add water and agitation and they cross-link into a continuous, elastic-yet-stretchy film. Too much glutenin behaviour and the dough is tight and tears; too much gliadin and it is a slack puddle. Good dough balances the two, and time plus water can do much of that linking for you without kneading at all.

blocks.caption: Build the net, then fill it with gas. Everything else is tuning.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.html: The reason a cold 48-hour ferment beats a warm 2-hour rise at the same final volume: rise measures only CO2 produced, but flavour comes from the other outputs of fermentation — organic acids, esters and alcohols — plus enzymatic breakdown of starch and protein into sugars and amino acids. Those accumulate on a slow clock that is largely independent of gas production. Long and cool means lots of flavour chemistry and modest gas; short and warm means the opposite. Same size, completely different dough.

Baker's percentage is the notation the whole field uses, and it is just ratios pinned to flour. Flour is always 100%. Every other ingredient is expressed as a percentage of flour weight — so 65% hydration means 65 g water per 100 g flour, whatever the batch. This is exactly your brew ratio: it travels between batch sizes and lets you compare two recipes at a glance. Two doughs at "1:0.65:0.02" are the same dough whether you mix 300 g or 3 kg of flour.

head: Ingredient
Baker's %
Role in the system
rows: The reference. Protein content sets gluten potential (bread flour ~12–14%, "00"/AP ~9–11%).
Hydration. Higher = more extensible, more open crumb, harder to handle.
Slows yeast, tightens gluten, seasons. Never zero.
Gas engine. Tiny numbers; more speeds the rise, not the flavour.
Wild yeast + lactobacilli. Replaces commercial yeast; adds acid and slows things down.

blocks.html: Total dough weight = sum of all the percentages. A 100/65/2/0.5 dough totals 167.5% of flour weight, so to hit ~800 g of dough (four ~200 g pizzas) you need 800 / 1.675 ≈ 478 g flour, and everything else falls out of that. This is the one arithmetic you will do forever.

items.title: Hydration
items.html: What: water as a % of flour. Why it matters: it is the single biggest lever on crumb — low (55–60%) gives a tight, easy-to-shape dough (bagels, sandwich, buns); high (70–85%) gives an open, airy, holey crumb (ciabatta, sourdough) but sticky, technique-hungry dough. Common mistake: jumping to 80% before you can handle 65% and concluding you "can't bake".

items.title: Gluten development
items.html: What: organising glutenin + gliadin into a strong, extensible film. Why it matters: no net, no gas retention, dense brick. Example: the windowpane test — stretch a walnut of dough thin enough to see light through without tearing. Common mistake: thinking only kneading builds gluten; time and hydration build it for free.

items.title: Fermentation (time × temp)
items.html: What: microbes eating sugars, producing gas + acids + alcohols. Why it matters: controls both rise and flavour, and the two are separable. Example: a cold retard at 4 °C / 39 °F for 24–72 h. Common mistake: chasing rise with more yeast and wondering why it tastes flat and yeasty.

items.title: Salt
items.html: What: ~2% of flour weight. Why it matters: it throttles yeast to a manageable rate, tightens the gluten so the dough holds shape, and is most of the seasoning. Common mistake: forgetting it — an unsalted dough over-ferments fast, spreads slack, and tastes of nothing. Also: dumping salt directly onto yeast in a concentrated slurry.

items.title: Bulk vs proof
items.html: What: bulk = the first rise of the whole mass; proof = the final rise after shaping. Why it matters: flavour and strength are built in bulk; oven-spring readiness is set in proof. Common mistake: conflating them, or degassing all the structure out between the two.

items.title: Surface tension & shaping
items.html: What: tightening the outer skin of the dough into a taut envelope. Why it matters: tension resists spread and forces the dough up in the oven (oven spring). Common mistake: punching high-hydration dough flat and destroying the gas cells you spent 24 h building.

blocks.label: Variable that matters
blocks.html: If you change only one thing this month, make it fermentation temperature and time, not the flour or the yeast brand. It is the highest-leverage, lowest-cost knob in the entire system and the one home bakers most consistently leave untouched.

blocks.title: Buy · Skip · Waste

rows.value: Digital scale to 1 g (ideally 0.1 g for salt/yeast) · large tub or bowl with lid · bench scraper · your oven's hottest setting
Baking steel (preferred) or stone · a way to launch (a peel, or an inverted tray)
Instant-read thermometer (dough + water temp) · Dutch oven (traps steam for hearth loaves) · proofing container with straight sides to read % rise
Stand mixer (convenient, not required — folds do the same job) · banneton (a bowl + tea towel + flour works) · lame (a razor on a stick; a sharp knife scores fine)
Bread machine · "pizza oven" gadgets that top out at 230 °C · dough conditioners and "improvers" · special bottled yeast nutrients

blocks.html: The scale is non-negotiable — baker's percentages are meaningless with volume measures, and a cup of flour varies ±20% by how you scoop it. Everything downstream (reproducibility, scaling, debugging) depends on weighing to the gram. Buy the steel over the stone: it has far higher thermal conductivity, so it dumps heat into the base of a pizza fast enough to crisp it before the top overcooks.
Three methods build the same net by trading labour for time. Pick one; they are interchangeable end-states.

1. Prep — weigh, don't measure. Set flour to 100% on the scale and derive water, salt, yeast from the percentages. Use warm-ish water (~26–28 °C / 79–82 °F) for room rises, cool for slow ones. Reasoning: temperature of the water is your fastest handle on fermentation speed.
  2. Execute — hydrate first (autolyse). Mix only flour + water, then rest 20–60 min before adding salt and yeast. The flour fully wets and enzymes begin linking gluten passively. Reasoning: much of the "kneading" happens for free during this rest; the dough after autolyse is already smoother.
  3. Execute — develop. Then either knead 8–10 min (mechanical), or do 3–4 sets of stretch-and-folds spaced 30 min apart during bulk (gentle, builds strength without a mixer), or simply wait 12–18 h (no-knead — time alone links the gluten). Reasoning: agitation and time are substitutes for the same cross-linking.
  4. Evaluate — windowpane + poke. Gluten: stretch a piece thin; translucent without tearing = developed. Ferment: dough has grown ~50–100% and a floured poke springs back slowly, leaving a slight dent. Reasoning: you are reading the dough's state, not the clock — the clock is only a prediction.
  5. Correction. Tears when stretched → under-developed, give it more folds or time. Springs back instantly and fights you → over-tight or under-rested, cover and wait 15–20 min for the gluten to relax before shaping.

1. Pre-shape & rest. Gently round each piece into a loose ball, rest 15–30 min covered. This relaxes gluten so the final shape doesn't fight back.
  2. Shape for tension. Fold the dough onto itself and drag it across an unfloured bench so the surface skin tightens into a taut dome. For pizza, keep the gas: press from the centre out and leave a puffy rim, never a rolling pin. Reasoning: surface tension is what converts fermentation gas into upward oven spring instead of sideways spread.
  3. Proof to just-under. Final rise until a poke springs back slowly but not fully. Slightly under-proofed is safer than over — under-proofed still springs in the oven; over-proofed collapses.
  4. Score, then bake hot with the right heat mode. Score hearth loaves to control where they burst. Bake bread with steam (Dutch oven lid, or a tray of water) for the first 15–20 min so the crust stays soft long enough to spring, then dry heat to set the crust. Pizza wants maximum heat — steel on the top rack under a blistering grill/broiler, 260 °C+ / 500 °F+. Reasoning: oven spring is a brief window; steam keeps the surface elastic while gas expands, then Maillard + caramelisation build crust colour and flavour.

blocks.label: Mediocre → Excellent
blocks.html: Mediocre pizza bakes at 220 °C on a cold tray: the base is pale and dries into a cracker before it can char. Excellent pizza launches onto a steel preheated 45–60 min at full heat with the grill on: the base sets and leoparding appears in 4–6 minutes, so the crust is crisp and the crumb stays open and moist. Same dough — the delta is entirely thermal mass and heat.

blocks.problem: Dense, tight loaf that barely rose

fields.detail: Under-developed gluten (no net), under-fermentation (not enough gas), dead/old yeast, or too much salt in contact with yeast early.
Did it pass the windowpane before shaping? Did bulk actually grow ~50%+? Proof yeast in warm sugared water — no foam in 10 min = dead.
Longer/warmer bulk, more folds, fresh yeast. Reserve full development before shaping; don't rush bulk to hit a clock time.

blocks.problem: Gummy, dense band near the base

fields.detail: Under-baked (starch not fully gelatinised/set), sliced while hot, or bottom heat too weak.
Internal temp of a lean loaf should hit 96–99 °C / 205–210 °F. If you cut it warm, the crumb "sets" as it cools — slicing early makes it gummy.
Bake longer / to temperature, bake lower in the oven or on a preheated steel, and cool fully (1 h+) before cutting.

blocks.problem: Dough won't stretch — it tears or snaps back

fields.detail: Snaps back = over-tight/under-rested gluten (too much glutenin behaviour, not relaxed). Tears = under-developed or too dry.
Snap-back that relaxes after 15 min = tension, not damage. Tears with a ragged edge = the net was never built, or hydration too low.
Snap-back: cover and rest 15–30 min, then shape. Tearing: more folds/time, or nudge hydration up 3–5% next batch.

blocks.problem: Over-proofed — dough collapsed, flat, sour, bursts randomly

fields.detail: Fermented too far: gluten exhausted, gas cells merged and popped, structure can no longer hold. Common with too much yeast + a warm kitchen + an unwatched clock.
Poke test: dent stays put and doesn't spring back at all; dough smells strongly boozy/sour and looks slack and bubbly-flat.
Can't reverse it — but you can rescue mildly over-proofed dough by gently re-shaping for fresh tension and baking immediately. Next time: less yeast, cooler ferment, or catch it earlier.

blocks.problem: Pale, soft crust with no colour

fields.detail: Oven not hot enough, too much steam left in for the whole bake, or fermentation ate all the residual sugars so there's nothing left to brown.
Crust colour is Maillard + caramelisation; both need heat and available sugar. Over-fermented dough browns poorly ("degassed of colour" too).
Hotter oven, remove steam/lid for the final third of the bake, and don't over-ferment. A touch of sugar or milk in enriched doughs helps browning.

blocks.problem: Pizza with a soggy, raw centre

fields.detail: Too many/too wet toppings, base not hot enough (no steel/stone, or under-preheated), or dough rolled too thin in the middle so sauce soaks through.
Lift the pizza — a pale, floppy underside means the base never got direct high heat before the top cooked.
Preheat steel 45–60 min at max, use less/drier sauce and pre-cook watery toppings (mushrooms, fresh mozzarella patted dry), and keep a slightly thicker centre.

blocks.html: One variable at a time, everything else fixed. Taste and photograph the crumb side by side — the differences are large and unmistakable.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E1 — the flavour lever

fields.detail: Prove that ferment time drives flavour independently of rise.
Same dough spec, same flour, same final dough ball size, same oven, same toppings.
Ferment schedule only: one batch same-day (2–3 h warm rise), one batch 48 h in the fridge at 4 °C / 39 °F. Pull the cold batch out 1–2 h before baking.
Similar final size and puff; the 48 h dough is markedly more complex, faintly tangy, browns better and blisters more.
Aroma of the raw dough (boozy/lactic in the cold batch), leoparding on the crust, and depth of flavour. This is the "restaurant pizza" reveal.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E2 — hydration & crumb

fields.detail: See how water alone reshapes crumb and handling.
Same flour, salt %, yeast %, ferment time and temp, same bake.
Hydration: one dough at 60%, one at 75%.
60% = firm, easy to shape, tighter even crumb. 75% = slack, sticky, needs wet hands and folds, but a far more open, glossy, irregular crumb.
How different they feel to handle, and the hole structure in cross-section. Learn which crumb you actually want before chasing extreme hydration.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E3 — salt as a throttle

fields.detail: Show salt is a fermentation brake and a structure agent, not just seasoning.
Same flour, hydration, yeast %, temperature, timing.
Salt: one dough at 2%, one at 0%. Watch both rise in identical containers.
Unsalted rises noticeably faster and further, then goes slack and sticky; salted rises slower, holds shape, tastes seasoned. Baked unsalted bread tastes flat and stales fast.
Rise rate over 90 min, slackness of the dough, and — crucially — the flavour gap in the finished loaf.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E4 — knead vs no-knead

fields.detail: Prove that time substitutes for kneading in building gluten.
Same 70% dough spec, same flour, same salt, same total dough weight and bake.
Development method: one kneaded 10 min then risen ~3 h; one mixed for 30 s then left 14–18 h (no-knead, less yeast).
Both windowpane and rise well; the no-knead often has a more open, irregular crumb and deeper flavour from the longer ferment.
Gluten strength before shaping and final crumb — you did zero kneading and still built a net.

sections.title: Practice system — the pizza dough spec

blocks.html: Master one dough by repetition before you sprawl. This is a genuinely usable Neapolitan-style home pizza dough, written as an engineer's spec. Learn to hit it every time, then perturb it.

blocks.title: SPEC · Cold-ferment pizza dough (4 × ~250 g balls)

rows.value: 378 g · cool, ~18 °C / 64 °F for a slow ferment
3 g · (use ~0.3% / 1.8 g if fermenting the full 72 h)

blocks.title: SCHEDULE · cold retard

rows.value: Autolyse flour + water 30 min, add salt + yeast, mix/fold to a rough smooth mass
1–2 h at ~21 °C / 70 °F with 2 sets of folds, until ~30% risen
Divide into 250 g balls, tuck tight, then 24–72 h at 4 °C / 39 °F
Out of fridge 1–2 h before baking; balls should be relaxed and puffy
Steel preheated 45–60 min at max + grill/broiler · 260 °C+ / 500 °F+ · 4–7 min

blocks.title: The reproducibility loop

fields.detail: Hit the same crumb and handling from the spec above three batches in a row.
Beginner → Consistent
Scale, the spec, a notebook.
Weigh precisely, log water temp + kitchen temp + total ferment time + final rise %, bake, photograph the crumb. Repeat, changing nothing.
Three near-identical results; you can predict the rise time from the temperature.
Wildly different rises = you're not controlling temperature/time. Log it and standardise.
Once boringly reproducible, change exactly one variable (E1–E4).

blocks.title: Shaping for tension

fields.detail: Build a taut, gas-retaining skin without degassing the dough.
Consistent → Optimization
An unfloured patch of bench, a bench scraper.
Pre-shape, rest 20 min, then drag-round each ball to a tight dome. Rest seam-down. For pizza, open by pressing centre-out, never rolling the rim flat.
A smooth taut surface that holds a dome and gives strong oven spring; a puffy leoparded pizza rim.
Ball slumps flat (no tension) or tears (over-tightened/dry). Adjust bench friction and rest time.
Move to higher hydration and keep the same tension — that is the real skill test.

blocks.title: Start and hold a sourdough culture

fields.detail: Raise a stable wild culture and learn to read its readiness.
Mastery
Wholemeal + white flour, water, a jar, scale.

Days 1–7: mix equal flour + water, discard and feed daily (e.g. 1:1:1 by weight) until it reliably doubles in ~4–8 h. Ready signs: predictable doubling, domed then peaked, passes the float test (a spoonful floats in water).
A starter that doubles on schedule and leavens a loaf without commercial yeast.
Sluggish = too cold or under-fed; hooch/liquid on top = hungry, feed more often; no rise after 2 weeks = start over warmer.
Tune feeding ratio (1:5:5 for a milder, slower starter) and temperature to steer sour intensity.

blocks.title: Homemade pizza night

fields.detail: Run the cold-ferment spec end to end and serve four pizzas that rival a good pizzeria.
Baker's %, cold fermentation, tension shaping, hot-steel bake, topping restraint.
A puffy, leoparded, blistered rim; a crisp base that stays open and moist; complex flavour from the 48 h ferment.
Lift a slice — the tip holds, the underside is charred not pale, the rim is airy not bready.

blocks.title: Burger buns (enriched dough)

fields.detail: Make a soft, tender enriched dough — lower hydration, with milk, butter, egg and a little sugar.
Enriched-dough handling (fat coats gluten, so develop before adding butter), dividing to uniform weights, egg-wash for shine.
Eight even, domed, glossy buns with a fine soft crumb that don't fall apart under a burger.
Uniform size (±5 g), even browning, tender not tough, tight enough crumb to hold juices.

blocks.title: Cinnamon rolls

fields.detail: Laminate a soft enriched dough with a butter-sugar-cinnamon filling, roll, cut and proof.
Rolling to even thickness, spiral shaping and tension, controlled proof, judging bake without a raw centre.
Soft, well-defined spirals, fully cooked to the middle, gooey filling, tender crumb.
Even spirals, no raw doughy core (probe ~90 °C / 194 °F centre), filling that stays put rather than leaking out entirely.

blocks.html: Sourdough capstone (L4): once the starter reliably doubles, bake a 75% hydration country loaf — autolyse, folds during bulk, cold retard overnight, bake in a preheated Dutch oven (lid on 20 min for steam, off 20–25 min to colour). This is where every concept in the module lands at once.

blocks.look: Look for: a thin translucent membrane you can see light through, stretched without tearing — that's a built net. Compare to a ragged tearing sheet (under-developed).

blocks.query: open crumb sourdough crumb shot high hydration
blocks.look: Look for: irregular, glossy, thin-walled holes of varying size — the signature of high hydration + good gas retention. Contrast with a tight even sandwich crumb.
Look for: a puffy blistered rim with dark leopard-spots — evidence of a well-fermented dough hit with very high heat. Pale flat rims mean cold oven or under-ferment.

blocks.query: bread oven spring scoring ear grigne
blocks.look: Look for: the raised "ear" where the score opened during oven spring — proof the dough had tension and wasn't over-proofed.

blocks.query: poke test proofing dough underproofed overproofed
blocks.look: Look for: the dent behaviour — springs back fast = under-proofed; springs back slowly leaving a slight dent = ready; stays fully dented = over-proofed.

blocks.html: Knowledge check — understanding, not recall. Answer in your own words; if you can explain the mechanism you own the concept.

questions: Two pizza doughs finish the same size, one after a 2 h warm rise and one after a 48 h cold ferment. Why does the cold one taste dramatically better if rise (gas) is equal?
You want a more open, holey crumb. Name the variable you'd change first and the handling cost that comes with it.
Your dough springs back and won't stretch. How do you tell "needs to rest" apart from "over-developed/torn", and what's the fix for each?
Why can a no-knead dough develop just as much gluten as a kneaded one? What is doing the work?
Convert this to gram weights for ~1000 g of dough: flour 100 / water 65 / salt 2 / yeast 0.5. Show the flour figure first.
Why is salt not optional, and what specifically goes wrong at 0%?

blocks.title: Same dough, two fates

fields.detail: Mix one batch of the pizza spec, split it, and ferment half same-day and half for 48 h cold. Bake both under identical conditions and taste side by side.
You can articulate the flavour and crust difference and tie each to a mechanism (acids/enzymes vs gas), and you nailed reproducibility on everything you held constant.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.html: Which of the four variables — hydration, development, fermentation, salt — did you find hardest to control this month, and what did the dough's behaviour (not the recipe) tell you when it went wrong? Write down the one measurement you'll start logging so that next month's failures become data instead of mysteries.
